title: Nanded, the last days
hook: tradition says he was stabbed by an assassin at Nanded and died of the wound

segments.voice: Yesterday, the white hawk on the Guru's hand, and the blue horse beneath him. Your line was the hawk and the horse. Did you see a bird come back to rest? Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

A river in the south, the Godavari, far from Punjab. A town on its bank called Nanded. Today there's a great white gurdwara there, and Sikhs travel a very long way to stand in it. Why so far from home? Because tradition says this is where the Tenth Guru's road ended. He had come south, a long way from Anandpur, and at Nanded he stopped. What happened there is told gently by Sikhs, and today we tell it the same way.
screen: `A RIVER IN THE SOUTH.` → `A TOWN CALLED NANDED.` → `WHERE THE ROAD ENDED.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells the last days in a few strokes. At Nanded, the Guru met an ascetic named Madho Das, living by the river. The meeting changed the man. He became a Sikh, took the name Banda Singh, and the Guru sent him north to Punjab. That is a story of its own, for another day. Then came the blow. Tradition says an assassin, a Pathan, came near the Guru and stabbed him. The wound was dressed and stitched. For a while it seemed he might recover. Then, the story goes, he drew a strong bow, and the stitches gave way. He knew his time was short. What did he do with it? This is the part Sikhs hold closest. He did not name another person to follow him. Instead, tradition says, he gathered his Sikhs and placed the Guru's authority where it would stay. Tomorrow we'll look at that carefully. Today, just notice the calm. A man who had lost his father, his mother and his four sons, who had fought and written and wandered, ends not in panic but in arranging what comes next. The place where he passed is now Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib, one of the seats of authority in Sikh life. Sachkhand means the realm of truth, the last of the realms in Guru Nanak's Japji. So the name itself says something. For Sikhs, the Tenth Guru's last place on earth points past the earth. Nanded is where the line of human Gurus came to its close, and where a new way of being guided was about to begin.
screen: `MADHO DAS BECOMES BANDA SINGH.` · `THE ASSASSIN, AND THE WOUND.` · `CALM, ARRANGING WHAT COMES NEXT.` · `SACHKHAND: THE REALM OF TRUTH.` · then, large: `THE LAST DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit quietly for him. Settle, and breathe. You don't need words. Just let the bare outline of his life pass through your mind: the boy at Anandpur, the hawk on his hand, the letters, the losses, the long road south, the river at Nanded. Then let it go still. If you pray, you can sit in Waheguru for him. If you don't, sit in plain respect for a life given all the way to the end. The bell holds the time.
Nanded. The town on the Godavari where, tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh was wounded and passed, now home to Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib. Today's word.
Your line: the last days. Today, pick one small thing you'd want settled if your time were short, and settle it. Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs travel to Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib at Nanded to remember the Tenth Guru's last days, and gurdwaras mark the anniversary of his passing with kirtan and Ardas.
